We are interested especially in the role of hydrogen molecules for the formation and evolution of primordial galaxies. Thus, the formation process of hydrogen molecules in a very low-metallicity galaxy (I Zw 18; the most typical metal-deficient galaxy) is studied. Adopting a recent observational result of the absorption lines of hydrogen molecules in I Zw 18, we obtain the upper limit for the ionization degree in the case where hydrogen molecules can form via the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}^{-}$</tex>-process, although they are generally believed to form on the surface of dust grains. Furthermore, we present a critical ionization degree, above which the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}^{-}$</tex>-process can be dominant over the formation process on the surface of grains. Interestingly, this critical ionization degree is comparable to the upper limit of the ionization degree for I Zw 18. For determining the formation process of hydrogen molecules, future observational facilities can be useful. Thus, we examine the detectability in some wavelengths for metal-deficient galaxies. According to our estimate, the near-infrared line emission of hydrogen molecules is observable at the level of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10\,\mu\rm{Jy}$</tex>, the free–free radio emission is at the level of mJy, and the far-infrared emission from the dust on which hydrogen molecules form can also be detected at the 10-mJy level with its temperature of 16 K. The near-infrared line and the far-infrared continuum are feasible for ASTRO-F observations.

articleTitle: Estimation of Central Black Hole Masses in Low-Luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We analyzed six low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (hereafter LLAGNs), which consist of two bright LINERs (low-ionization nuclear emission line region) with broad H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, and of four bright low-luminosity Seyferts observed by the X-ray satellite ASCA. We examined the time variabilities of these targets, and found that most targets show no significant time variabilities, although these galaxies belong to LLAGNs. By applying Fourier analysis to their light curves in the 2–10keV band, we obtained the lower limits of their time variability scales, which correspond to their central black hole masses greater than several times <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{6}\,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. Our result suggests that these LLAGNs are harbors of super-massive black holes, but the emitting powers are only <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< 1 \%$</tex> of the Eddington luminosities of the central engines in the LLAGNs due to their small accretion rates. Since a black hole would grow by mass accretion, it is hard to create such a super-massive black hole under a small accretion rate. Therefore, the mass-accretion rates in the past must have been larger than those at present, and the galaxies have probably been as luminous as QSOs. This will be a hint to find out the cause of the lack of QSOs in the local universe.

articleTitle: An Abundance Study in the Hg-Mn Star 46 Aquilae (HD 186122) with the SUBARU/HDS
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A detailed abundance analysis has been carried out for the Hg-Mn star 46 Aql using high-resolution spectra in the visual region (5100–6400 Å) obtained with the High Dispersion Spectrograph of the Subaru Telescope. Our attention has been mainly focused on those elements which have not been analyzed previously. He, C, N, and O are underabundant, while Na shows the solar abundance. We have confirmed previously reported underabundances of Mg, Al, and Si, and have found an overabundances of P (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+1.5\,\rm{dex}$</tex>) and Ti (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+1.0 \,\rm{dex}$</tex>) and a significant underabundance of S (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-1.8 \,\rm{dex}$</tex>). Fe is overabundant by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+0.8 \pm 0.1 \,\rm{dex}$</tex> and a microturbulent velocity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.3 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> was found from an analysis of the Fe ii lines. Among a few hundred unidentified absorption lines, we identified lines of As ii and Xe ii and a very large (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+4.0 \,\rm{dex}$</tex>) overabundance of Xe is obtained. We have confirmed emission lines of Mn ii and Ti ii near 6100 Å, while those of Cr ii cannot have been seen.

articleTitle: A Hyperenergetic CO Shell in the Galactic Center Molecular Cloud Complex
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the detection of a high-velocity feature, CO 1.27<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.01, in the Galactic-center molecular-cloud complex. In our <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO images taken with the NRO 45 m telescope, CO 1.27<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.01 appears as the second prominent high-velocity feature, next to CO 0.02–0.02, having a velocity width of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta V \simeq 100 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> and a size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$9 \,\rm{pc} \times 12 \,\rm{pc}$</tex>. It seems to consist of two expanding shells with sizes of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10 \,\rm{pc}$</tex>. The major shell has a kinetic energy of about an order of magnitude larger than the gravitational energy, indicating that the shell is apparently gravitationally unbound. We propose that CO 1.27<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.01 may have been accelerated by a series of supernova explosions which occurred within the last <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 6 \times 10^4 \,\rm{yr}$</tex>. No association of a nonthermal radio continuum source suggests a strong magnetic field (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B \gtrsim 0.4 \,{\rm mG}$</tex>) in the vicinity of CO 1.27<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>0.01.

articleTitle: Near-Infrared Observations of S 255-2 : The Heart of a Massive YSO Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: High-resolution near-infrared (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L^\prime$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M^\prime$</tex>) images of a massive star-forming region, S 255-2, were obtained with the Subaru Telescope and an infrared camera, CIAO. These images clearly resolve two sets of bipolar nebulae illuminated by two independent massive YSOs. A number of cluster member YSOs have been detected, including 3 new sources. Seven early-B type stars have been identified within 10 pc of S 255-2; three are associated with extended optical H II regions. The variation in the appearance of these early-B type stars suggests an evolutionary sequence of massive stars in the S 255 region.

articleTitle: ASCA Observation of the Millisecond Pulsar PSR J2124$-$3358
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The isolated 4.9 ms pulsar PSR J2124<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>3358 was observed with ASCA on 1998 May 9, and the X-ray spectrum in the 0.5–10 keV band was obtained. The X-ray spectrum can be fitted with a single blackbody model with a temperature <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT = 0.31^{+0.08}_{-0.06}\,\rm{keV}$</tex>, although a simple power-law model with a relatively large photon index <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma = 2.8^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$</tex> cannot be rejected.

articleTitle: Radiatively-Driven Relativistic Accretion Disk Winds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We theoretically examined relativistic disk winds driven by disk radiation fields. For the present purpose, we quantitatively caluculated the full components of radiation fields produced by a standard accretion disk around Schwarzschild and extreme Kerr black holes, under the pseudo-Newtonian gravity and special relativity. The typical strength of radiation fields of disks around the Schwarzschild hole reduces by about 50%, whereas that around the extreme Kerr hole increases by about ten times, as compared with the Newtonian case. We found that the wind is easy to blow off from the disk around the Kerr hole, although it becomes difficult from the disk around the Schwarzschild hole, as long as the accretion rate is subcritical. In the extreme Kerr case the maximum terminal speed is about <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.5c$</tex> for the critical accretion rate.

articleTitle: An X-Ray Emitting Supernova Remnant Candidate, M 33 X-4
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Based on ASCA observations of the Local-Group spiral galaxy M 33, a report is made on the X-ray properties of luminous X-ray source called X-4, which is located in a giant H ii region in M 33. The 0.8-8.0keV spectrum of X-4 is described by a two-component model, consisting of a thin thermal plasma emission with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.0 \,\rm{keV}$</tex>, and a power law emission with a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 2.0$</tex>. The two spectral components cross over at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 3.0 \,\rm{keV}$</tex>. These spectral properties are similar to those of a young supernova remnant (SNR), except that the 0.8-8.0keV luminosity of M 33 X-4, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.0 \times 10^{38} \,\rm{erg} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, is considerably higher than those of the SNRs in the Milky Way. There is also evidence of excess absorption, or an over-abundance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>-elements relative to iron. If this source is an SNR, the hard component is thought to be synchrotron radiation from high-energy particles, produced either by shock acceleration, like in SN 1006, or by a central neutron star, like in the Crab Nebula.

articleTitle: Nucleosynthesis inside Supernova-Driven Supercritical Accretion Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have investigated nucleosynthesis in a supercritical accretion disk around a compact object of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.4\,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, using the self-similar solution of an optically thick advection dominated flow. Supercritical accretion is expected to occur in a supernova with fallback material accreting onto a new-born compact object. It has been found that appreciable nuclear reactions take place even for a reasonable value of the viscosity parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_{\rm{vis}} \simeq 0.01$</tex>, when the accretion rate <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{m} = \dot{M}c^2/(16 L_{\rm{Edd}}) \gt 10^5$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm{Edd}}$</tex> is the Eddington luminosity. If <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{m} \ge 4 \times 10^6$</tex>, all heavy elements are destroyed to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{4\atop} \rm{He}}$</tex> through photodisintegrations at the inner part of the disk. Even <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{4\atop} \rm{He}}$</tex> is also disintegrated to protons and neutrons near the inner edge when <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{m} \ge 2 \times 10^7$</tex>. If the fallback matter of the supernova explosion has the composition of a helium-rich layer of the progenitor, a considerable amount of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${{44\atop} \rm{Ti}}$</tex> could be ejected via a jet from the disk.

articleTitle: The r-Process Nucleosynthesis in Neutrino-/Magnetocentrifugally-Driven Winds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We consider the effects of the rotation and magnetic fields on the rapid neutron capture nucleosynthesis (r-process nucleosynthesis) in neutrino-driven winds. We examine the features of steady and subsonic wind solutions which extend the model of Weber and Davis (1967, Astron. Jahresber. 67.6776), which is a representative solar-wind model. Then, we find that the entropy per baryon becomes lower and the dynamical timescale becomes longer as the angular velocity becomes higher. The results are inappropriate for the production of r-process nuclei. Therefore, we conclude that it is difficult to realize a successful r-process nucleosynthesis in this framework.

articleTitle: Intracluster Supernova as a Possible Extra Energy Source of Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The observed luminosity–temperature relation of clusters is considerably steeper than that expected from a simple scaling relation. Although extra energy input is a likely solution, its source has not been identified. We propose intracluster supernova as a possible source, and also predict the supernova rate in intracluster space as a critical test.

articleTitle: SiO Maser Survey of Southern IRAS Sources
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have surveyed 163 southern IRAS sources in the SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=2$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1 v=1$</tex> maser line at 86 GHz, obtaining 38 (22 new and 16 previously known) detections. These detections include 6 stars not previously detected in OH 1612 MHz surveys, and 4 sources assigned incorrect OH radial velocities. The distance reachable in this survey turned out to be about 4 kpc. The local velocity dispersion near the Sun were found to be approximately <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$30~\rm{km}~\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> for these IRAS/SiO sources. A relatively high concentration of the SiO detected sources were found at the area <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$320{{}^{\rm{\circ}}} \lt l \lt 340{{}^{\rm{\circ}}}$</tex> (toward “Norma tangent”). The estimated distances for these sources suggest that this concentration is spread between 2 and 6 kpc from the Sun, peaking on the Scutum–Crux arm.

articleTitle: How Evolved are the Mass Donor Stars in Cataclysmic Variables?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Recent spectroscopic observations have identified several cataclysmic variables non-solar metal abundances. We present theoretical models which examine the level of core evolution expected for CV secondaries prior to contact. Our results indicate that few secondary stars evolve past 10% of their main sequence lifetime prior to the initiation of mass transfer; a result of which is in agreement with present day observations. Thus, the non-solar metal abundances observed must be due to nuclear burning by-products accreted by the secondary star during common envelope sweeping prior to initial contact or ejecta collected during classical nova outbursts.

articleTitle: CO ($J=6-5$) Observations of the Quasar SDSS 1044$-$0125 at $z = 5.8$
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a result of CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=6-5$</tex>) observations of a quasar SDSSp J104433.04<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>012502.2 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 5.8$</tex>. Ten days of observations with the Nobeyama Millimeter Array yielded an rms noise level of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 2.1 \,\rm{mJy}\;\rm{beam}^{-1}$</tex> in a frequency range from 101.28 GHz to 101.99 GHz at a velocity resolution of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$120 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>. No significant clear emission line was detected in the observed field and frequency range. The three-sigma upper limit on the CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=6-5$</tex>) luminosity of the object is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.8 \times 10^{10} \,\rm{K} \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1} \,\rm{pc}^2$</tex>, corresponding to a molecular gas mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.2 \times 10^{11} {{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, if a conversion factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4.5 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}} (\rm{K} \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1} \,\rm{pc}^2)^{-1}$</tex> is adopted. The obtained upper limit on the CO luminosity is slightly smaller than those observed in quasars at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=4-5$</tex> toward which CO emissions are detected.

articleTitle: An Extremely Red Nucleus in an Absorbed QSO at z=0.65
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The results of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K$</tex>-band-imaging observations of a candidate of an absorbed QSO at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z=0.653$</tex>, AX J131831+3341, are presented. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ B-K$</tex> color of the object is 4.85 mag, which is much redder than optically-selected QSOs. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K$</tex>-band image shows nuclear and extended components, the same as in the optical <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V$</tex>-, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R$</tex>-, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ I$</tex>-band images. The nuclear component (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ I-K = 4.29$</tex> mag) is much redder than the power-law models with energy indices of 0 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-1.0$</tex>, which well reproduce the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V-R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R-I$</tex> optical colors of the nuclear component. A heavily absorbed (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ A_V \sim 3$</tex> mag) nucleus may emerge in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K$</tex>-band, while optical light may originate from scattered nuclear light. The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ I-K$</tex> color of the extended component is 2.2 mag, which is consistent with the post-starburst nature of the host galaxy, which is also suggested from the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ V-R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ R-I$</tex> colors of the extended component.

articleTitle: Bondi Accretion onto a Luminous Object
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Spherical accretion of ionized gas onto a gravitating object is examined under the influence of central radiation. In classical Bondi accretion onto a non-luminous source with mass <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex>, the accretion rate <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}_{\rm B}$</tex> is expressed as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}_{\rm B} = \lambda (\gamma) \times 4 \pi G^2 M^2 \rho_\infty c_{\rm s} {\infty ^{-3}}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rho_\infty$</tex> is the density at infinity and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_{\rm{s}\infty}$</tex> the sound speed at infinity. We first found that the normalized accretion rate <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda(\gamma)$</tex> is approximated by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda(\gamma) = -(5/4)\gamma+ (19/8)$</tex>, instead of a rigorous expression. When the central object is a “spherical” source, the accretion rate <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex> reduces to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}_{\rm B} (1-\Gamma)^2$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma$</tex> is the central luminosity normalized by the Eddington one. If the central luminosity is produced by the accretion energy, the steady canonical luminosity is determined and the normalized luminosity does not exceed unity, as expected. On the other hand, when the central object is a “disk” source, such as an accretion disk, the accretion rate becomes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}/\dot{M}_{\rm B} = 1 -2 \Gamma_{\rm d} + (4/3) \Gamma_{\rm d}^2$ </tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm d} > 1/2$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}/\dot{M}_{\rm B} = 1 /(6\Gamma_{\rm d})$</tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm d} > 1/2$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Gamma_{\rm d}$</tex> is the normalized disk luminosity. We also found steady canonical solutions, where the normalized luminosity can exceed unity for sufficiently large accretion rates. The anisotropic radiation field of accretion disks greatly modifies the accretion nature.

articleTitle: The Fundamental Plane of Spiral Galaxies: Search from Observational Data
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The fundamental plane of spiral galaxies was searched from observational data, which can be approximately represented in observational parameters by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L \propto V^2 R$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L, R$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex> are the luminosity, the linear size of galactic disk, and the rotation velocity. This plane exists at all optical bands in our samples of more than 500 spiral galaxies in total. It is more fundamental than the relationship between any two of the parameters, and can reduce the residual of the Tully–Fisher <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex> relations by about 50%. Noticed that the power index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex> is doubled from that of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex>, which implies that the total mass and the mass distribution of galaxies plays an important role in forming the fundamental plane. Involving the third parameter of galactic size has a strong physical implication on galaxy formation and the dark-mass distribution.

articleTitle: Changing Supercycle of the ER UMa-Type Star V1159 Ori
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examined the VSNET light curve of the ER UMa-type star V1159 Ori. We detected a large variation of the supercycle (the interval between successive superoutbursts) between extremes of 44.6 and 53.3d. The outburst activity was also found to decrease when the supercycle was long. The observed variation of the supercycle corresponds to a variation of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 40\%$</tex> of the mass-transfer rate from the secondary star, totally unexpected for this class of objects. We also detected a hint of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1800 \,\rm{d}$</tex> periodicity in the variation, whose period is close to what has been suggested for solar-type cycles for cataclysmic variables (CVs). If this periodicity is caused by the magnetic activity of the secondary star, this detection constitutes the first clear evidence of continuing magnetic activity in CV evolution, even after crossing the period gap. This activity may partly explain still poorly understood origins of the high mass-transfer rates in ER UMa-type stars.

articleTitle: ASCA Observations on Two Molecular Cloud Cores in the Perseus Complex
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present ASCA results for two molecular cloud cores in the Perseus complex, Barnard 1 and a cloud core which contains a class 0 protostar, IRAS 03282<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3035. Four X-ray sources are found, of which two have either a radio, infrared, or optical counterpart. The X-ray temperature and flux of an IRAS source, IRAS 03275<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3020/AX J0330<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3030, are similar to those of T Tauri stars. Thus, together with the infrared and optical data, this source can be classified as a T Tauri star. Two unidentified sources have a spectrum with moderate temperature and absorption, and are possibly new young stellar objects in the clouds. A radio source, BWE 0328<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3054/AX J0331<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3104, has a hard X-ray spectrum fitted with a power-law model of photon index <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.5$</tex>, and hence would be an active galactic nucleus. No X-ray emission is found from a class 0 protostar, IRAS 03282<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3035, and a class 0 candidate, IRAS 03301<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>3057.

Author Keywords: ISM: individual objects (Perseus Molecular Cloud Complex)

articleTitle: First Results of a CO Survey of the Small Magellanic Cloud with NANTEN
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the first results from a new <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{-} 0$</tex>) survey of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) with the NANTEN millimeter-wave telescope. The survey covered the northeast and southwest regions of the main Bar, and the H ii regions N 84, N 88 in the Wing at a linear resolution of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 50 \,\rm{pc}$</tex>. Twenty-one giant molecular clouds (GMCs), whose masses are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10^{4} \hbox{-} 10^{6} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, were identified. Significant CO emission, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm R}^{\ast} \sim 0.36 \, {\rm K}$</tex>, was first detected toward the N 84 region in the Wing, which is comparable to those of the prominent CO clouds associated with infrared sources LIRS 36, LIRS 49 in the Bar. The GMCs exhibit a good spatial correlation with the H ii regions and young clusters, indicating that cluster formation is on-going in these GMCs. On the other hand, they show little correlation with older clusters or with supernova remnants, suggesting rapid dissipation of CO.

articleTitle: ASCA Observations of the BL Lacertae Object OJ 287 in 1997 April and November
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The X-ray properties of the BL Lacertae object OJ 287, observed with ASCA on 1997 April 26 and November 17, are reported. The 0.5–10 keV flux was lower than that obtained in previous X-ray observations, and no evidence of intensity variations was found during each observation. The obtained flux densities at 1 keV, 0.22–0.26 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu\mathrm{Jy}$</tex>, exceed the extrapolations from lower frequency synchrotron continua, which were measured in nearly the same period as the present ASCA observations. The X-ray spectra acquired with the GIS and SIS were consistently described with a single power-law model modified by the Galactic absorption, and the derived photon indices, 1.5–1.6, are flatter than those observed so far. These results strongly suggest that the X-ray spectra observed in 1997 arise via an inverse Compton process alone. The X-ray spectra obtained in 1994 (Idesawa et al. 1997, AAA 68.159.334), exhibiting a steeper slope than those in 1997, is thought to be contaminated by a “synchrotron soft tail.”

articleTitle: Stability of the GJ 876 Planetary System
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The newly discovered planetary system of the GJ 876 is stabilized by a 2:1 mean-motion resonance. We carried out numerical simulations of the GJ 876 planetary system for several sets of initial epochs, and investigated their stability, since this planetary system is very sensitive to an initial epoch because of a large difference between the osculating elements and the mean elements.

articleTitle: The 1996–1997 Fading of V651 Monocerotis, the Binary Central Star of the Planetary Nebula NGC 2346
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: V651 Mon is the binary central star of the bipolar planetary nebula NGC 2346. The star showed the second-ever deep fading in 1996–1997, which was presumably caused by obscuration by a dust cloud in the planetary nebula, as was proposed to explain the 1981–1985 event. The entire duration of the 1996–1997 event was <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 400 \,\rm{d}$</tex>, remarkably shorter than the 1981–1985 event, suggesting that the obscuring body was smaller or had a larger tangential velocity. The most remarkable feature in this event was the presence of a sharply defined transient clearing (brightening). From the time-scale of the variation, we propose an upper limit of the projected scale of several times <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10^{11} \,\rm{cm}$</tex> of the structure responsible for the brightening. This observation provides the first evidence for a sharply defined, small lucent structure within the obscuring body around the central star of NGC 2346.

articleTitle: The X-Ray Structure of the Supernova Remnant 3C 400.2
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present here the results of an X-ray study of the supernova remnant 3C 400.2 (G53.6-2.2) using the ASCA data. 3C 400.2 has an unusual morphology at radio wavelengths, suggesting two SNRs superposed along the same line of sight, whereas its X-ray emission is known to be centrally peaked. We investigated the X-ray spectral variation across the remnant using the ASCA GIS and the ROSAT PSPC data. The X-ray spectra can be well fitted by thin thermal plasma models. However, there is no significant variation in the temperature and the ionization parameter across the remnant. We conclude that it is a single SNR rather than two overlapping SNRs. The centrally peaked X-ray morphology and the thin thermal emission with nearly cosmic abundances indicate that 3C 400.2 belongs to a class of “mixed-morphology SNRs”. We found that the physical parameters of 3C 400.2 are similar to those of other mixed-morphology SNRs. The morphology of 3C 400.2 can be explained by a supernova explosion occurring near to the edge of an interstellar cloud.

articleTitle: Hoyle–Lyttleton Accretion onto Superdisks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion onto superdisks, where the mass-accretion rate greatly exceeds the critical one and the luminosity is of the order of the Eddington one. Hoyle–Lyttleton accretion onto a luminous accretion disk is drastically changed from the spherical case, due to the non-spherical nature of disk radiation fields. In edge-on accretion, for example, mass accretion does not cease at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma=1$</tex>, but continues in the regime of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma \geq 1$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma$</tex> is the disk luminosity normalized by the Eddington one. We found that Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion onto superdisks is not a simple extension of that onto standard accretion disks, where the mass-accretion rate gradually decreases with increasing <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma$</tex>. Instead, in the case of a superdisk, the mass-accretion rate increases with increasing <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma$</tex>. This is due to a geometrical shadowing effect. That is, in contrast to the infinitesimally-thin standard disk, the superdisk has finite thickness. As <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \Gamma$</tex> increases, the relative thickness increases and the shadowing region in the equatorial direction increases. We also briefly discuss the canonical luminosity in the steady state and the system evolution.

articleTitle: Hipparcos Proper-Motion System with Respect to SPM 2.0
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: On the basis of Hipparcos data, whose system is believed to be quasi-inertial to within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm 0.25 \,\rm{mas} \,\rm{yr}^{-1}$</tex> and to represent an internally consistent reference frame, we carried out an analysis of the SPM 2.0 proper-motion system. Comparing the Hipparcos proper motions with those of the SPM 2.0 Catalog, which provides absolute proper motions of objects measured directly relative to external galaxies, we found that the two components of the spin vector, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega_x$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega_z$</tex>, are apparently less than the value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.25 \,\rm{mas} \,\rm{yr}^{-1}$</tex> for the uncertainty of the Hipparcos inertiality, while the component <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\omega_y$</tex> is almost twice that value. Inspecting the magnitude - and color-dependent pattern of the proper-motion difference, we found that the SPM 2.0 Catalog seems to suffer a slight color systematics with respect to the Hipparcos proper-motion system, though the result is inconclusive due to the small number of the Hipparcos and SPM 2.0 common stars.

articleTitle: Basic Properties of Thin-Disk Oscillations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper oscillations on geometrically thin disks are reviewed, focusing on two issues. One is the characteristics of disk oscillations. The other is possible excitation mechanisms of these oscillations. The main purpose of this paper is to clarify the physics and dynamics involved in these issues. We consider both Newtonian and general-relativistic disks, since a comparison of the oscillations on both disks clarifies the differences among these two oscillations and is helpful for understanding the unique properties of relativistic disks. Furthermore, we sometimes refer to stellar oscillations, since a comparison with stellar oscillations is helpful to have a deeper understanding of the disk oscillations, especially of the excitation mechanisms.

articleTitle: Exploring Galaxy Evolution from Infrared Number Counts and Cosmic Infrared Background
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Recently reported infrared (IR) galaxy number counts and cosmic infrared background (CIRB) all suggest that galaxies have experienced strong evolution sometime in their lifetime. We statistically estimate the galaxy evolution history from these data. We find that an order-of-magnitude increase of the far-infrared (FIR) luminosity at redshift <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z = 0.5$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 1.0$</tex> is necessary to reproduce the very high CIRB intensity at 140 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \mu m$</tex> reported by Hauser et al. (1998, AAA 070.161.559) and decreases to, even at most, a factor of 10 toward <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z \sim 5$</tex>, though many variants are allowed within these constraints. This evolution history also satisfies the constraints from the galaxy number counts obtained by IRAS, ISO and, roughly, SCUBA. The rapid evolution of the comoving IR luminosity density required from the CIRB well reproduces the very steep slope of galaxy number counts obtained by ISO. We also estimate the cosmic star formation history (SFH) from the obtained FIR luminosity density, considering the effect of the metal enrichment in galaxies. The derived SFH increases steeply with redshift in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 0 < z < 0.75$</tex>, and becomes flat or even declines at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z > 0.75$</tex>. This is consistent with the SFH estimated from the reported ultraviolet luminosity density. In addition, we present the performance of the Japanese ASTRO-F FIR galaxy survey. We show the expected number counts in the survey. We also evaluate how large a sky area is necessary to derive secure information of galaxy evolution up to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ z \sim 1$</tex> from the survey, and find that at least <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 50$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 300\;\mathrm{deg}^2$</tex> is required.

articleTitle: CO Survey of Nearby Spiral Galaxies with the Nobeyama 45-m Telescope: II. Distribution and Dynamics of Molecular Gas
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have studied the distribution and dynamics of molecular gas in galaxies by observing CO emission mainly along the major and minor axes of 28 nearby spiral galaxies with the 45-m telescope of the Nobeyama Radio Observatory. The observations showed that the surface density of molecular gas indicates an exponential distribution in the region of the flat (differential) rotation curve for all spiral galaxies. This could be because the radial distribution is determined by gas inflow due to the viscosity of molecular clouds. The surface density of molecular gas in barred galaxies also shows a characteristic distribution in the region of the bar, suggesting gas inflow along the bar by the bar potential and perpendicular to the bar by viscosity. Such a transfer of molecular gas increases the gas density in the central region, probably causing the evolution of the rotation curve, which is determined by the mass distribution, on the time scale of the galaxy age. We compared the radial distribution of the surface density of H I with that of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}_{2}$</tex>, and found same scale length of the exponential distribution in the Virgo galaxies and a much larger scale length in field galaxies for H I. This could be due to a difference in the viscosity coefficient of the H I gas.

articleTitle: Study of Molecular Clouds and Star Formation in the Region of IC 2118
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO survey of molecular clouds in the region of the reflection nebula IC 2118. Our observations covered the whole area of IC 2118 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 6 \,\rm{deg^2}$</tex>) with a 2.<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime}$</tex>6 beam at a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4^{\prime}$</tex> grid spacing. We identified six molecular clouds. Based on a literature search we found a distance value of 210 pc for the reflection nebula and its associated molecular clouds, indicating that the clouds are probably interacting with the Orion–Eridanus Bubble. Using this distance value, we determined the physical properties of the clouds. We also made an objective prism search for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\rm H} \alpha$</tex> emission stars in the region in order to find possible solar-type stars born in the clouds, and identified 46 candidate pre-main-sequence stars. Their spectroscopic follow-up is in progress. Seven of them have so far proved to be T Tauri stars.

articleTitle: Possible Kreutz Sungrazing Comets Found in Historical Records
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In historical records, twenty four candidates of possible Kreutz sungrazing comets have been found, and their times of perihelion passage estimated. Translated original records of comets with presumed ephemerides are given. Some uncertain candidates are also presented. Although already suggested by Marsden (1967, Astron. Jahresber. 67.9133), our calculations on the motions of comets 1882 R1 and 1965 S1 confirm that the progenitor of these comets is a comet that appeared in 1106; some trials on the linkage of sungrazing comets are discussed.

articleTitle: 12CO Molecular Cloud Survey and Global Star Formation in Lupus
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The Lupus star-forming region has been surveyed for molecular clouds in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO with the NANTEN radio telescope, and a cloud mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.7 \times 10^{4} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> has been revealed. We were able to detect 105 molecular clouds, most of which are relatively small and of low mass. The members of the Sco OB 2 association and the X-ray detected pre-main-sequence stars (PMSs) are distributed all around this region. The OB stars and the molecular clouds show exclusive distributions. Large fractions of the PMSs are located away from the molecular clouds, and are thus isolated. The origin of the isolated PMSs is discussed. About 40% of the PMSs have candidates of their parent clouds less massive than 20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex> within 4 pc, which suggests in-situ star formation in the small clouds and their rapid dissipation. The separations from the PMSs to the clouds are typically larger than those in the Chamaeleon region, probably because of coexisting OB stars. From the cloud structures and the distributions of the OB stars, PMSs, and H i expanding shell, it is suggested that the molecular clouds have been effectively dissipated by the OB stars and a shock wave, which may also have triggered star formation in Lupus and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rho$</tex> Oph clouds.

articleTitle: Nonlinear Stochastic Biasing of Peaks and Halos: Scale-Dependence, Time-Evolution, and Redshift-Space Distortion from Cosmological N-body Simulations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have quantified the degree of nonlinearity and stochasticity of the clustering of biased objects using cosmological <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body simulations. Adopting the peaks and the halos as representative biasing models, we focused on the two-point correlation of the biased objects, dark matter and their cross-correlation. Especially, we took account of the effect of redshift-space distortion and attempted to clarify the scale dependence and the time dependence by analyzing the biasing factor and the cross-correlation factor. On small scales, stochasticity and nonlinearity become appreciable and strongly object-dependent, especially in redshift space due to the pair-wise velocity dispersion of the biased objects. Nevertheless, an approximation of deterministic linear biasing, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta_{\rm obj}\simeq b_{\rm obj} \delta_{\rm mass}$</tex>, works reasonably well even in the quasi-linear regime, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r \gtrsim 10\,h^{-1} {\rm Mpc}$</tex>, and linear redshift-space distortion explains the clustering amplitudes in redshift space in this regime.

articleTitle: Stability of Terrestrial Protoplanet Systems and Alignment of Orbital Elements
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The dynamical characteristics of terrestrial protoplanet systems have been investigated. Diagrams which show the instability timescale of terrestrial protoplanet systems as a function of the protoplanet separation (we call them CWB diagrams) were analyzed and interpreted. We have produced CWB diagrams for several different initial parameters, mainly with perturbations from Jupiter and Saturn. One-peakedness of the diagrams for small random velocity cases is interpreted from the viewpoint of orbital alignment in protoplanets. The orbital alignment serves as a stabilizer of the protoplanet system by preventing particles from making close encounters. Terrestrial protoplanet systems appear to be most stable where the tidal force produced by perturbers and mutual gravitational interaction among particles balance; in such cases, orbital alignment is realized. Thus, the terrestrial protoplanet systems turn out to be another example of the so-called secular orbit-orbit resonance frequently found in planet-satellite or satellite-ring systems. Gradual breaking of the orbital alignment invokes an instability in protoplanet systems, which can lead to the collisional evolution of protoplanets into the present planets.

articleTitle: Propagation of Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Rays from Sources in the Super-Galactic Plane
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have performed detailed numerical simulations on the propagation of UHE protons in the energy range <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E = (10^{19.5} \hbox{-} 10^{22.0}) \, {\rm eV}$</tex> in a relatively strong extragalactic magnetic field with a strength of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B = (10 \hbox{-} 100) \,\rm{nG}$</tex> within about 40Mpc. In this case, the deflection angles of UHECRs become so large that the no counterparts problem can be simply solved. As for the source distribution, we assumed that it is proportional to the number distribution of galaxies within the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin sphere. We found many clusters, meaning small-scale anisotropy, in our simulations. It has also been shown that the observed energy spectrum is well reproduced in our models without any fine-tuned parameter. We used the correlation value in order to investigate statistically the similarity between the distribution of arrival directions of UHECRs and that of galaxies. We found that each correlation value for each parameter set begins to converge when the number of detected events becomes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$O(10^3)$</tex>. Since the expected number counts by the experiment of the next generation, such as TA, HiRes, Auger, and EUSO, are thought to be on the order of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^3$</tex>, we will be able to check in the very near future whether the source distribution of UHECRs is correlated with the Super-Galactic Plane or not. Compared with the AGASA data, a significant anisotropy on the arrival directions of UHECRs is found in the analyses of the first and second harmonics. This may originate from an incompleteness of the ORS database. This problem may also be solved if the source distribution is slightly changed. For example, this problem may be solved if we assume that UHECRs come from some galaxies, such as AGNs and radio galaxies.

articleTitle: ASCA Observation of the Superluminal Jet Source GRO J1655–40 in the 1997 Outburst
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the results of an ASCA observation of the Galactic jet source GRO J1655–40 performed from 1997 February 25 to February 28 covering a full orbital period (2.62 d). The averaged 2–10 keV flux was about 1.1 Crab. An absorption line feature centered at 6.8 keV was detected both in the GIS and SIS spectra. We interpret this as a blend of two resonance-absorption <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{K}\alpha$</tex> lines from H-like and He-like iron ions. We can consistently explain both the ASCA spectra and the simultaneous RXTE/PCA spectrum by a combination of K-absorption lines and K-absorption edges of iron ions. The fact that the absorption line is stably present over the whole orbital phase implies that the distribution of the highly ionized plasma is not affected by the companion star, which is consistent with its presence around the black hole. A curve of growth analysis shows that the plasma contains velocity dispersion along the line-of-sight larger than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$300~\rm{km}~\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> attributed to bulk motions. It is probably a part of a geometrically thick accretion flow in turbulent motions with velocities of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$500$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1600~\rm{km}~\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> at an estimated radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim10^{10}~\rm{cm}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Water-Vapor Maser Emission from the Seyfert 2 Galaxy IC 2560: Evidence for a Super-Massive Black Hole
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present an H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser emission study of the Seyfert galaxy IC 2560 based on single-dish and VLBI observations. The maser emission was detected in multiple velocity ranges: one around the systemic velocity, one blue-shifted from the systemic velocity by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim220$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$420~$</tex>km<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$~$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and one red-shifted by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim210$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$350~$</tex>km<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$~$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. This was the first detection of high-velocity features in this galaxy. The velocity of the systemic features drifts at a mean rate of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.62\pm0.09~$</tex>km<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$~$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}~$</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Assuming a compact Keplerian disk at the nucleus, the inner and outer radii of this disk are 0.07 and 0.26 pc, respectively. The central mass confined within the disk inner radius is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.8\times10^6~M_{\odot}$</tex>, and its density is at least <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.1\times10^9~M_{\odot}~\hbox{pc}^{-3}$</tex>. Such a high density strongly suggests the existence of a black hole at the nucleus. The maser spots of the systemic features are distributed over <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lt 0.3~$</tex>mas (0.04 pc). The continuum source at the same position as the maser source is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lt 1.0~$</tex>mas (0.13 pc) in size, and its brightness temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.7\times10^{11}~$</tex>K confirms IC 2560 to be an AGN. The 2-10 keV luminosity based on ASCA data is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.0\times10^{41}~$</tex>erg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$~$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, which makes IC 2560 one of the low-luminosity AGNs. Adopting the standard accretion model, the mass-accretion rate needs to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2\times10^{-5}~M_{\odot}~\hbox{yr}^{-1}$</tex> in order to explain the X-ray luminosity.

articleTitle: ASCA Temperature Maps of Three Clusters of Galaxies: Abell 1060, AWM 7, and the Centaurus Cluster
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present two-dimensional temperature maps of three bright clusters of galaxies (Abell 1060, AWM 7, and the Centaurus cluster), based on multi-pointing observations with the ASCA GIS. The temperatures were derived from hardness ratios by taking into account the XRT response. For the Centaurus cluster, we subtracted the central cool component using the previous ASCA and ROSAT results, and the metallicity gradients observed in AWM 7 and the Centaurus cluster were included in deriving the temperatures. The intracluster medium in Abell 1060 and AWM 7 is almost isothermal from the center to the outer regions with temperatures of 3.3 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.9$</tex> keV, respectively. The Centaurus cluster exhibits remarkable hot regions within about <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${30{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> from the cluster center, showing a temperature increase of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+0.8$</tex> keV from the surrounding level of 3.5 keV, and the outer cool regions with lower temperatures by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-1.3$</tex> keV. These results imply that a strong merger has occurred in the Centaurus in the recent 2–3 Gyr, and that the central cool component has survived it. In contrast, the gas in Abell 1060 was well-mixed in an early period, which probably has prevented the development of a central cool component. In AWM 7, mixing of the gas should have occurred in a period earlier than the epoch of metal enrichment.

Author Keywords: galaxies: clusters: individual (Abell 1060, AWM 7, Centaurus Cluster)

articleTitle: JHK Spectra of the z = 2.39 Radio Galaxy 53W002
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present low-resolution, near-IR JHK spectra of the weak <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=2.39$</tex> radio galaxy 53W002, obtained with the OH-airglow Suppressor spectrograph (OHS) and Cooled Infrared Spectrograph and Camera for OHS (CISCO) on the Subaru Telescope. They cover rest-frame wavelengths of 3400–7200Å, and the emission lines of [O II]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda$</tex>3727, H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>, [O III]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda\lambda$</tex>4959, 5007, H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, [N II]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda\lambda$</tex>6548, 6583 and [S II]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda\lambda$</tex>6716, 6731 were detected. Using the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>/H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> line ratio, we find an extinction of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E(B\hbox{-}V)=0.14$</tex>. The emission-line ratios are reproduced by a cloud of electron density <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm{e}}=1\times 10^{3-4}\,\rm{cm}^{-3}$</tex> with solar metallicity, ionized by an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha=-0.7$</tex> power-law continuum with ionizing parameter <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U=1\times 10^{-3}$</tex>. In addition to these emission lines, we make the first spectroscopic confirmation of the Balmer discontinuity in a high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> radio galaxy. Together with rest-frame UV photometry from the literature, we show that at least 1/3 of the present stellar mass was formed in the current starburst. The stellar mass was estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(1\hbox{-}1.4)\times10^{11}\,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> by one-component model fitting, which is smaller than that of typical <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z\sim 1$</tex> B2/6C radio galaxies. We suggest that 53W002 is currently assembling a large part of its stellar mass through merger events with the surrounding sub-galactic clumps, some of which can be identified with the L<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emitters detected in narrow-band imaging. After a few such events over the next few Gyr, 53W002 will evolve into a massive elliptical galaxy.

articleTitle: Detecting Galactic MACHOs with VERA through Astrometric Microlensing of Distant Radio Sources
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We consider the properties of astrometric microlensing of distant radio sources (QSOs and radio galaxies) due to MACHOs, and discuss their implications for VERA (VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry). First, we show that in the case of astrometric microlensing of distant sources, the event duration is only a function of the lens mass and tangential velocity, but independent of the lens distance, in contrast to the well-known three-fold degeneracy for photometric microlensing. Moreover, the lens mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex>, is scaled by the tangential velocity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v_\perp$</tex>, as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M\propto v_\perp$</tex>, rather than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M\propto v_\perp^2$</tex>, which is the case for photometric microlensing. Thus, in astrometric microlensing the dependence of the lens mass on the unknown parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v_\perp$</tex>, is weaker, indicating that the duration of an astrometric microlensing event is a better quantity to study the mass of lensing objects than that of photometric microlensing. We also calculate the optical depth and event rate, and show that within 20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^{\rm{\circ}}$</tex> of the galactic center a typical event rate for a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10~\mu\rm{as}$</tex>-level shift is larger than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.5 \times 10^{-4}$</tex> event per year, assuming that a quarter of the halo is made up of MACHOs. This indicates that if one monitors a few hundred sources for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20 years, such an astrometric microlensing event is detectable. Since a typical event duration has been found to be fairly long (5 to 15 years), the frequency of the monitoring observation can be relatively low, i.e., once per six months, which is rather reasonable for practical observations. We discuss a practical strategy for observing astrometric microlensing with VERA, and argue that an astrometric microlensing event due to MACHOs can be detected by VERA within a few decades.

articleTitle: Seyfert-Type Dependences of Narrow Emission-Line Ratios and Physical Properties of High-Ionization Nuclear Emission-Line Regions in Seyfert Galaxies
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to examine how narrow emission-line flux ratios depend on the Seyfert type, we compiled various narrow emission-line flux ratios of 355 Seyfert galaxies from the literature. We present in this paper that the intensity of the high-ionization emission lines, [Fe VII]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda6087$</tex>, [Fe X]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda6374$</tex>, and [Ne V]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda3426$</tex>, tend to be stronger in Seyfert 1 galaxies than in Seyfert 2 galaxies. In addition to these lines, [O III]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda4363$</tex> and [Ne III]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda3869$</tex>, whose ionization potentials are not high (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$< 100 \, {\rm eV}$</tex>), but whose critical densities are significantly high (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gtrsim 10^7 \, {\rm cm}^{-3}$</tex>), also exhibit the same tendency. On the other hand, the emission-line flux ratios among low-ionization emission lines do not show such a tendency. We point out that the most plausible interpretation of these results is that the high-ionization emission lines arise mainly from highly-ionized, dense gas clouds, which are located very close to nuclei, and thus can be hidden by dusty tori. To examine the physical properties of these highly-ionized dense gas clouds, photoionization model calculations were performed. As a result, we find that the hydrogen density and the ionization parameter of these highly-ionized dense gas clouds are constrained to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H} > 10^6 \, {\rm cm}^{-3}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U > 10^{-2}$</tex>, respectively. These lower limits are almost independent both from the metallicity of gas clouds and from the spectral energy distribution of the nuclear ionizing radiation.

articleTitle: Photospheric Abundances of Volatile and Refractory Elements in Planet-Harboring Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: By using the high-dispersion spectra of 14 bright planet-harboring stars (along with 4 reference stars) observed with the new coudé echelle spectrograph at Okayama Astrophysical Observatory, we investigated the abundances of volatile elements (C, N, O, S, Zn; low condensation temperature <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm c}$</tex>) in order to examine whether these show any significant difference compared to the abundances of other refractory elements (Si, Ti, V, Fe, Co, Ni; high <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm c}$</tex>), which are known to be generally overabundant in those stars with planets, since a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm c}$</tex>-dependence is expected if the cause of such a metal-richness is due to the accretion of solid planetesimals onto the host star. We found, however, that all elements which we studied behave themselves quite similarly to Fe (i.e., <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$[\rm{X} / \rm{Fe}] \simeq 0$</tex>), even for the case of volatile elements. This may suggest that the enhanced metallicity in those planet-bearing stars is not so much an acquired character (by accretion of rocky material) as rather primordial.

articleTitle: Kashima 34-m Water Maser Survey of Late-Type Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: This paper presents new results of a water maser survey of late-type stellar objects at 22.235 GHz with the Kashima 34-m radio telescope. We have detected 179 out of 643 observed sources, including 32 new detections. The sources were selected in terms of the IRAS flux density and colors of late-type stars, involving optically observable Mira/semiregular variables, IRC objects, OH/IR sources and protoplanetary nebulae. We found the highest <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}_{2}\rm{O}$</tex> detection rate for the type of stars with a thin dust envelope (Mira/semiregular variables) among other types of sources. This is attributed to the smaller distances to such stars in the sample. The velocity spread of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}_{2}\rm{O}$</tex> maser profile has an increasing tendency with the IRAS color, though it becomes more difficult to access this color dependence beyond an edge of the transition of the (oxygen-rich) Asymptotic Giant Branch stars to protoplanetary nebulae in the two-color diagram.

articleTitle: Dust–Gas Accretion onto a Luminous Object
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Spherical accretion of dust and gas onto a gravitating object is examined under the influence of central radiation. We found that, as long as the central luminosity is less than the Eddington one for dust, the gas flow is almost Bondi type, while the dust flow is greatly affected by central radiation. For non-luminous sources, in the outer region where the gravity on the dust is balanced by the drag force, the infall velocity of dust is generally larger than the gas velocity. Both gas and dust freefall in the inner region. As the dust-to-gas ratio increases, the gas accretion rate slightly decreases, while the dust accretion rate increases. As a result, the total accretion rate increases. When the central luminosity is considered, the infall velocity of dust becomes smaller and smaller, as the central luminosity increases. Although the gas accretion rate slightly increases with luminosity, the dust accretion rate linearly decreases due to the radiation pressure. As a result, the total accretion rate decreases with luminosity. Approximate expressions for dust and gas accretion rates were obtained.

articleTitle: CO Survey of Nearby Spiral Galaxies with the Nobeyama 45-m Telescope: I. The Data
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We mapped the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 -0$</tex>) emission along the major and minor axes of disks or bars of 25 nearby galaxies using the Nobeyama 45-m telescope with a spatial resolution of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.01$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.12 D_{25}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D_{25}$</tex>: de Vaucouleurs’ diameter), and detected the CO emission at 8–42 positions along each axis. The galaxy sample includes morphological type Sab and Scd as well as barred and nonbarred. These data are useful to statistically study the internal distribution and dynamics of molecular gas in galaxies and to deduce common characteristic properties. In this paper, we describe the sample and observations, present all spectra and measured line parameters, and examine the relations between the global molecular gas mass and the Hubble type, the total mass of the galaxies, and the star-formation rate.

articleTitle: NIR Narrow- and Broad-Band Study of the SSA 22 Field
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Deep narrow- and broad-band near-infrared imaging observations of the central <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${2{}^{\rm {\prime }}} \times {2{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> region of the SSA 22 field were made with the near-infrared camera (CISCO) attached to the Subaru Telescope. Using a narrow-band filter centered at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.033\, {\mu \rm {m}}$</tex>, [O III] <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda~5007$</tex> emitters at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 3.06 \pm 0.02$</tex> were searched to examine star-forming activities in an over-density region where a clustering of Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) and Lyman <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emitter candidates around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 3.09$</tex> was reported, though the targeted redshift is slightly different from that of the peak of the over-density region. Although one emitter candidate at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 3.06$</tex> was detected, it is likely to be located at a redshift of between 1 and 2 judged based on multi-band photometry. Another emission-line object was detected in another narrow-band filter (“off band” filter) centered at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.120\, {\mu \rm {m}}$</tex>, which is identified with a galaxy at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z = 0.132$</tex> (the emission line is Paschen <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>). The <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^{\prime}$</tex>-band imaging data revealed the presence of 12 Extremely Red Objects (EROs) with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$I_{814}-K^{\prime} \geq4$</tex>.
