The distribution of the EROs does not seem to coincide with that of Lyman Break Galaxies or Lyman <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim3$</tex>. The magnitudes and colors of the EROs are not consistent with those of passively evolving massive elliptical galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim3$</tex>. Candidates for counterparts of the submm sources detected with SCUBA are found; no EROs around the submm sources are found in our magnitude limit.

articleTitle: VLBI Monitoring Observations of Water Masers around the Semi-Regular Variable Star R Crateris
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We monitored water-vapor masers around the semi-regular variable star R Crateris with the Japanese VLBI Network (J-Net) at the 22 GHz band during four epochs with intervals of one month. The relative proper motions and Doppler-velocity drifts of twelve maser features were measured. Most of them existed for longer than 80 days. The 3-D kinematics of the features indicates a bipolar expanding flow. The major axis of the asymmetric flow was estimated to be at P.A.<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$= 136^{\circ}$</tex>. The existence of a bipolar outflow suggests that a Mira variable star had already formed a bipolar outflow. The water masers are in a region of apparent minimum radii of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.3 \times 10^{12} \,\rm{m}$</tex> and maximum radii of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.6 \times 10^{12} \,\rm{m}$</tex>, between which the expansion velocity ranges from 4.3 to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$7.4 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>. These values suggest that the water masers are radially accelerated, but still gravitationally bound, in the water-maser region. The most positive and negative velocity-drifting features were found relatively close to the systemic velocity of the star. We found that the blue-shifted features are apparently accelerated and the red-shifted apparently decelerated. The acceleration of only the blue-shifted features seems to be consistent with that of the expanding flow from the star.

articleTitle: Near-IR Observations of IRAS Sources with SiO Masers at the Inner Galactic Bulge
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Near-infrared photometric observations in the J-, H-, and K-bands have been made for 86 IRAS sources toward the inner Galactic bulge (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert l\vert \lt 3{{}^{\rm{\circ}}}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert b\vert \lt 3{{}^{\rm{\circ}}}$</tex>). SiO maser emission has previously been detected in all of these sources; they are well-confirmed, mass-losing, late-type stars having accurate radial velocities derived from SiO observations. For 78 sources, single, unambiguous near-infrared counterparts were found within the errors of the IRAS positions; for the other 8 sources, multiple candidates, candidates with a low confidence level, or candidates overlapped with other stars were found. From the J-, H-, K-band and IRAS 12 and 25 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\mu \rm {m}}$</tex> intensities, we estimated the spectral energy distributions of the sources, and obtained the distances, assuming a constant luminosity. The derived distances of the IRAS/SiO sources are consistent with the current bar model of the Galactic bulge, where the near side of the bar is located in the first quadrant of the galactic longitude. We also reanalyzed the radial velocity shift with distance, and confirmed the presence of streaming motions of stars in the bar-like bulge.

articleTitle: Dynamic Current Injection into Magnetic Loops in Active Regions I. Supplies of Energy and Mass to Active-Region Corona in the Form of Dynamic Loop Brightenings
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: One of the discoveries by Yohkoh is that a large part of the soft X-ray emission from the active-region corona comes from hot gas injected dynamically into magnetic loops from below. We propose that the major part of the supply of energy and mass to active region corona may be due to a dynamical leakage of magnetic twists produced in the subphotospheric convection layer. These twists naturally propogate out along the magnetic field to the active region corona as a large-amplitude torsional Alfvén-wave packet (TAWP, equivalent to a coaxially self-closed packet of MHD current), and the active-region corona is a dumping ground for such currents. These TAWP’s, which are passively produced in the dominant gas motion in the convection layer, dynamically influence the lower pressure gas as they propagate out into the chromosphere and the corona. The flux tube in the corona is pinched near the axis and heated. The pinched region propagates dynamically with the Alfvén velocity along the magnetic loop, driving the pinch-heated high-temperature gas into a spinning jet (a sweeping pinch). This may explain the supply of energy and mass to active-region corona in the form of the active-region loop brightenings found by Yohkoh.

articleTitle: A New Look at CO Outflows in the Dark Cloud Complex near IC 5146
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: This paper presents the results of a search for CO outflows in a dark cloud complex near IC 5146 carried out using the 45-m telescope at Nobeyama Radio Observatory (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{HPBW} = 17^{\prime\prime}$</tex>) equipped with the S115Q multi-beam receiver system. A CO outflow was discovered by the present survey toward IRAS 21428<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>4732, whose physical parameters, such as molecular mass, mechanical momentum, and kinetic energy, were derived. In addition to IRAS 21428<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>4732, there are 5 other IRAS point sources accompanied by CO outflows in this cloud complex, which were found by earlier observations with lower angular resolutions (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{HPBW} \simeq 1^\prime$</tex>). We also made <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup> CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1-0$</tex>), <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1-0$</tex>), and C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>O (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1-0$</tex> observations toward the 5 sources with the 45-m telescope in order to obtain new data with higher angular resolutions. CO maps as well as physical parameters of these outflows obtained by the 45-m telescope are also presented.

articleTitle: A CO Survey of the LMC with NANTEN: II. Catalog of Molecular Clouds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: From a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=1 \hbox{-} 0$</tex>) survey with the NANTEN telescope, we present a complete catalog of giant molecular clouds (GMCs) in the Large Magellanic Cloud. In total, 107 CO clouds have been identified, 55 of which were detected at more than 3 observed positions. For the 55 clouds, the physical properties, such as size, line-width, virial mass, and CO luminosity, are cataloged. From a statistical analysis of these quantities, we show that GMCs in the LMC are close to gravitational equilibrium. A comparison with H i data indicates that most of the CO clouds are distributed in dense parts of H i gas, whose H i column density is greater than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{21} \,\rm{cm}^{-2}$</tex>. It is notable that the mass ratio of the molecular-to-atomic hydrogen of the lower radial velocity component of gas is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.2$</tex>, which is a factor of 2 higher than that of the gaseous-disk component, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.1$</tex>. Molecular clouds are apparently formed efficiently in the parent atomic clouds in the lower velocity component. The CO Arc, which is a few kpc scale ordered structure of CO clouds along the southern optical edge of the galaxy, corresponds well to the the lower velocity component of H i gas.

articleTitle: When Did the Hubble Sequence Appear?: Morphology, Color, and Number-Density Evolution of the Galaxies in the Hubble Deep Field North
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using the HST WFPC2/NICMOS archival data of the Hubble Deep Field North, we constructed a nearly complete sample of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{V} \lt-20$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim L^\ast +1$</tex>) galaxies to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=2$</tex>, and investigate when the Hubble sequence appeared, namely, the evolution of the morphology, colors, and the comoving number density of the sample. Even if taking into account the uncertainty of the photometric redshift technique, the number density of relatively bright bulge-dominated galaxies in the HDF-N decreases significantly at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \gt 1$</tex>, and their rest-frame <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U-V$</tex> color distribution is wide-spread over <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.5 \lt z \lt 2$</tex>. On the other hand, while the number density of both disk-dominated and irregular galaxies does not show a significant change at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.5 \lt z \lt 2$</tex>, their distribution of the rest-frame <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U-V$</tex> color alters at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 1.5$</tex>; there is no relatively red (rest <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$U-V \gtrsim 0.3$</tex>) galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \gt 1.5$</tex>, while a significant fraction of these red disk-dominated or irregular galaxies exist at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \lt 1.5$</tex>. These results suggest that the significant evolution of the Hubble sequence, which is seen in the present Universe, occurs at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1 \lt z \lt 2$</tex>.

articleTitle: ASCA Observations of the Central Regions of M 31
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Using ASCA, spatially integrated X-ray spectra of the central regions of M 31 were studied. Data were accumulated over three different circular regions, with radii of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3', 6'$</tex>, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$12'$</tex>, all centered on the nucleus. The spectra are relatively similar among the three regions. In the energy range above 1.5 keV, the spectra are reproduced by a combination of a disk black-body component and a black-body component, implying that the emission mainly comes from an assembly of low-mass X-ray binaries. At energies below 1.5 keV, the spectra involve two additional softer components, expressed by thin-thermal plasma emission models of temperatures of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.9 \,\rm{keV}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.3 \,\rm{keV}$</tex>. Over the central <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$12'$</tex> (2.4 kpc) region and in the 0.5–10 keV energy band, the binary component has a luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.6 \times 10^{39} \,\rm{erg} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, while the two softer components both exhibit luminosities of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 2 \times 10^{38} \,\rm{erg} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>. These results are compared with those from other missions, including Chandra and XMM-Newton in particular. A discussion is presented on the nature of the two softer spectral components besides the binary one.

articleTitle: Study of the Long-Term X-Ray Variability of a Possible Quasar RX J0957.9+6903 with ASCA
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The long-term variability and spectral properties of a possible quasar, RX J0957.9+6903, were studied utilizing 16 ASCA observations spanning 5.5 years. The average 0.7–10 keV spectrum of RX J0957.9+6903 is well represented by a power-law continuum having a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 1.58 \pm 0.03$</tex> and an absorption column of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim 1 \times 10^{21}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$</tex>. The 2–10 keV flux of RX J0957.9+6903 varied by a factor of four over a period of six years, around a mean of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim 8.8 \times 10^{-12}~\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$</tex>. Peak-to-peak variability within each observation was less than 25% on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sim 1$</tex> day time scale. These properties support the classification of RX J0957.9+6903 as a quasar. The power spectrum density (PSD) was estimated in a “forward” manner over a frequency range of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 10^{-8.2}$</tex>-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 10^{-4.3}$</tex> Hz by utilizing the structure function method and a Monte Carlo simulation assuming a broken power-law type PSD. Then, the break frequency <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ f_\mathrm{b}$</tex> of the PSD of RX J0957.9+6903 has been constrained as 1/<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ f_\mathrm{b} = 1600^{+\infty}_{-1100}$</tex> days, and the logarithmic slope of the high-frequency region of the PSD as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \alpha =-1.55 \pm 0.2$</tex>. A comparison of the estimated PSDs is made between RX J0957.9+6903 and the M81 nucleus, observed in the same field of view.

articleTitle: Theoretical Models of Multi-Waveband QSO Luminosity Functions
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The cosmological evolution of the QSO luminosity functions (LFs) at NIR/optical/X-ray bands for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.3 \lesssim z \lesssim 3.5$</tex> is discussed based on realistic QSO spectra. The accretion-disk theory predicts that although the QSO luminosities only depend on the mass-accretion rate, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex>, the QSO spectra have dependence on the black-hole mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm BH}$</tex>, as well. The smaller is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm BH}$</tex> and/or the larger is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex>, the harder does the QSO NIR/optical/UV spectrum become. We modeled the disk spectra which can reproduce these features, and calculated the LFs for a redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 3$</tex> with the assumption of new-born QSOs shining at the Eddington luminosity. The main results are: (i) the LFs observed at optical and X-ray bands can be simultaneously reproduced. (ii) LFs in the optical and X-ray bands are not sensitive to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm{BH}}$</tex>, while LFs at the NIR bands are; about a one order of magnitude difference is expected in the volume number densities at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{I, J} \sim 10^{46} \,\rm{erg} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> between the case that all QSOs would have the same spectral shape as that of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm BH} = 10^{9} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> and the case with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm BH} = 10^{11} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. (iii) The resultant LFs at NIR are dominated by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{7} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> black holes at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{I, J} \lesssim 10^{44} \, {\rm erg} \, {\rm s}^{-1}$</tex>, and by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{11} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> black holes at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{I, J} \gtrsim 10^{46} \, {\rm erg} \, {\rm s}^{-1}$</tex>. Future infrared observations from space (e.g. NGST) will probe the cosmological evolution of black-hole masses. For a redshift of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \lt 3$</tex>, on the other hand, the observed optical/X-ray LFs can be fitted if the initial QSO luminosity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_0$</tex>, is below the Eddington luminosity, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm Edd}$</tex>. Interestingly, the best-fitted values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ell \equiv L_0/L_{\rm Edd}$</tex> are different in the B- and X-ray bands; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\ell_{B} \approx 2.5 \, \ell_{\rm x}$</tex>. The reason for this discrepancy is briefly discussed.

articleTitle: The Most Luminous Protostars in Molecular Clouds: A Hint to Understand the Stellar Initial Mass Function
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The maximum luminosity of protostars forming in molecular clouds has been investigated as a function of the parent cloud mass on the basis of a rich cloud sample searched for in the literature. In total, we gathered 499 molecular clouds among the published data, out of which 243 clouds were found to be associated with protostellar candidates selected from the IRAS point-source catalog. A diagram of the maximum stellar luminosity in each cloud and the parent cloud mass shows that the protostars in the clouds associated with H II regions are apparently more luminous than those in clouds away from H II regions over the entire cloud mass range investigated (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ 1 < M_\mathrm{CL}/M_{{\odot }} < 10^6$</tex>). In addition, we found that there are well-defined upper and lower limits in the maximum stellar luminosity distribution with the lower limit having a steeper dependence on the cloud mass (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L_\mathrm{MAX} \propto M_\mathrm{CL}^{1.5}$</tex>) than the upper one (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ L_\mathrm{MAX}\propto M_\mathrm{CL}^{0.8}$</tex>). All of these features can be naturally accounted for if we assume that the luminosity function of protostars is controlled by the cloud mass and the external pressure imposed on the cloud surface. We introduce a simple model for the stellar luminosity function as a function of these quantities, which should be closely related to the stellar initial mass function.

articleTitle: A 12CO $J = 1 \hbox{-} 0$) Survey of Molecular Clouds toward the Vela Supernova Remnant with NANTEN
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The molecular distribution toward the whole extent of the Vela SNR has been obtained at a linear resolution of 0.15 pc in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{-} 0$</tex>) emission with the NANTEN telescope. The CO distribution is generally anti-correlated with the SNR. The X-ray distribution has a sharp boundary toward the CO clouds, especially in the east, suggesting an interaction between them. There is only weak CO emission in the west, and the X-ray emission extends smoothly toward this direction. This indicates that the absence of dense gas probably allowed hot gas to escape freely. The CO clouds are highly filamentary, exhibiting a spatial correlation with regions of optical shocked features on a large scale. In the north of the SNR, enhanced X-ray emission is found toward network-like optical filaments. We suggest that this enhancement is due to the evaporation of molecular gas by shock heating caused by the interaction between the blast wave and the molecular gas. Comparisons with a few simple theoretical models of SNR evolution and expansion indicate that the clouds are mostly pre-existent, are being accelerated, and are evaporating now.

articleTitle: The 2000–2001 Superoutburst of the WZ Sge-Type Star RZ Leonis: A Clue to Understanding the Origin of Viscosity in Quiescent Dwarf Nova Disks
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report here on time-resolved photometric observations of the superoutburst of a dwarf nova, RZ Leo, which occurred during 2000 December–2001 January. We reveal the following characteristics of the outburst based on our observations: long duration, large amplitude, and the existence of two types of superhumps — “early superhumps” and “normal superhumps”. In addition to the extremely low frequency of the outbursts, the characteristics of the outburst strongly indicate that RZ Leo is the fifth member of the WZ Sge-type dwarf novae.The orbital period of RZ Leo is 0.07651 d, which is remarkably longer than the “canonical” period of other WZ Sge stars (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.058\,\rm{d}$</tex>). The longer period indicates a non-degenerate secondary of RZ Leo, which suggests that the idea of a low quiescence viscosity due to a degenerate brown dwarf secondary may not be correct. The present discovery of RZ Leo as being a WZ Sge star provides the first clear indication that the decay of magnetic turbulence in accretion disks of quiescent WZ Sge stars plays an important role in producing the proposed low quiescent viscosity.

articleTitle: A Large-Scale Study of H13CO+ and C18 (J=1–0) in Orion B
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have made a new survey for dense cloud cores in the Orion B region using the NANTEN telescope. Two molecular transitions, the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 - 0$</tex> line of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}{{13\atop} \rm{CO}}^{+}$</tex> and the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 - 0$</tex> line of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex>, were used to study the distribution of dense molecular gas with densities of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{4} - 10^{5} \,\rm{cm}^{-3}$</tex>. We detected 19 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> clumps, and the mass and the size of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> clumps ranged from 13<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex> to 990<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex> and from 0.26 pc to 0.69 pc, respectively. Among the physical parameters of these <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> clumps, the molecular column density, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N(\rm{H}_2)$</tex>, has been found to be the best indicator of star formation; the molecular column density averaged within a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> clump shows a good correlation with the IRAS luminosity as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm IRAS} / {{{L}_{\odot}}} \propto N({\rm H}_{2}) \; ({\rm cm}^{-2})^{4.8 \pm 0.6}$ </tex> (C.C.<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$= 0.96$</tex>). We also detected 11 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}{{13\atop} \rm{CO}}^{+}$</tex> clumps, whose mass ranges from a few <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex> to 480<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${M}_{\odot}$</tex>. Five of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}{{13\atop} \rm{CO}}^{+}$</tex> clumps are of smaller mass, and show no indication of massive star formation; they were newly found in this survey. Five of the eleven <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}{{13\atop} \rm{CO}}^{+}$</tex> clumps are particularly massive with an average mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 200 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. It is found that these massive <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{H}{{13\atop} \rm{CO}}^{+}$</tex> clumps exhibit active formation of massive stars, as indicated by associated protostellar IRAS point sources, whose luminosities are <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{2} - 10^{4} \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex>.

articleTitle: A Large Scale 12CO (J=1−0) Survey toward the Chamaeleon Region with NANTEN
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out a large-scale survey for molecular clouds in <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1-0$</tex>) emission toward the Chamaeleon region with the NANTEN 4-meter radio telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile. The survey covered <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 491 \,\rm{deg}^2$</tex> toward <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$284 {{}^{\circ }} \lesssim l \lesssim 320 {{}^{\circ }}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-34 {{}^{\circ }} \lesssim b \lesssim-6 {{}^{\circ }}$</tex> at an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$8^{\prime}$</tex> grid spacing. The total molecular mass in the observed area is estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 8300 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. More than 60% of the total mass is concentrated in and around the previously known Cha I, II, and III dark clouds. Two cloud complexes having molecular hydrogen masses of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 430 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1300 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, respectively, have been found at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10 {{}^{\circ }}$</tex> galactic-east of the Chamaeleon major clouds. We have identified a prominent filament extending from Cha I to the galactic-east direction, which is remarkably long (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gtrsim 40 \, {\rm pc}$</tex>) compared with filamentary features found in other dark-cloud complexes. A correlation study between the CO distribution and isolated X-ray emitting T Tauri stars (TTSs) indicates that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gtrsim 65\%$</tex> of the TTSs are located within 1 pc of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO cloud boundaries. This suggests that low-density parental molecular gas still remains around the isolated TTSs, although the dense parts with density greater than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^3 \, {\rm cm}^{-3}$</tex> have almost dissipated. This provides further support for the local formation of “isolated” T Tauri stars in small clouds.

articleTitle: Study of L 688/L 694/L 700: a Complex of Dark Clouds in Aquila
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of optical and radio molecular observations of the small dark clouds L 688, L 694, and L 700 (CB 200). Based on star counts, we found a distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$230 \pm 30\,\rm{pc}$</tex> for the clouds. We present extinction maps of the clouds based on the USNO Catalog data. Our objective prism search for candidate pre-main-sequence stars resulted in the detection of an <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\rm H} \alpha$</tex> emission star in the cloud area. We observed the clouds in the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1\hbox{-}0$</tex>), and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1\hbox{-}0)$</tex> lines. A ring-shaped cloud of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 430\,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> was detected from the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO observation. Five <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>CO cores were identified. Three <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> cores with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N(\rm{H}_{2}) \sim (5.3\hbox{-}7.6) \times 10^{21}\rm{cm}^{-2}$</tex> reside in two of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>CO cores in the northern part of the cloud. The density gradient seen in optical, infrared and radio, and also the positions of the star-formation sites may suggest the possibility of shock compression due to some stars or SNRs near the galactic plane.

articleTitle: Galaxy Population in a Cluster of Galaxies around the Radio Galaxy 3C 324 at $z=1.2$
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We discuss the properties of galaxies around the radio galaxy 3C 324 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=1.2$</tex> based on <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$BVRIK^\prime$</tex> multi-band imaging data. We have applied a photometric-redshift technique to objects in the 3C 324 field, and identified 35 objects as plausible cluster members. We have found that red and luminous members are concentrated in a small region enclosed by a circle of 40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> radius (0.33Mpc at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=1.2$</tex> for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Omega_0 = 0.3, \lambda_0 = 0.7, H_0 = 70 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1} \,\rm{Mpc}^{-1}$</tex> cosmology) from the 3C 324 galaxy. The 3C 324 cluster is probably much more compact in size compared with the local clusters. We constructed a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^\prime$</tex>-band luminosity function of the cluster members and fitted a Schechter function, and found the characteristic magnitude to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^{\ast\prime}_{\rm AB} = 20.2 \pm 0.6$</tex>. This value is consistent with the extrapolation of the pure passive evolution seen for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \lt 1$</tex> clusters. We have identified eight bright galaxies which form a red color–magnitude sequence. The slope of the sequence is consistent with the passive evolution model down to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^{\prime}_{\rm AB} \lt 22$</tex>; we also found that there is no clear age variation in these bright red galaxies. However, seven out of these eight galaxies exhibit a significant excess in the rest UV light with respect to the passive evolution model. This may suggest that the massive early-type galaxies in this high-redshift cluster are still forming stars to some extent. We have confirmed a truncation of the color–magnitude sequence at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^{\prime}_{\rm AB}\sim 22$</tex>; faint passively-evolving galaxies may not yet be present in this cluster at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \sim 1.2$</tex>. The overall color distribution of the cluster members, selected by the photometric redshift technique, is found to be very broad. We derived the fraction of blue galaxies in this cluster following a definition of Butcher and Oemler (, AAA 038.160.068), and obtained <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$f_{\rm B} = 0.39 \pm 0.28$</tex>, which is higher than that for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z \lt 1$</tex> clusters. This indicates that the star-formation activity of this cluster is, on the average, higher than that of lower redshift counterparts.

articleTitle: X-Ray Microlensing of Bright Quasars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We calculated the expected microlens light curves for several accretion-flow models and compared the results to find what aspects of distinct flow structures can be extracted from the microlens light curves. As for the flow models, we considered the standard disk, optically thin advection-dominated flow, and the disk-corona model by Kawaguchi et al., which can nicely reproduce the observed quasar spectra. The calculated microlens light curves of the disk-corona model exhibit rapid soft X-ray and slow hard X-ray variations. This is because the former is generated by Compton up-scattering of soft (optical–UV) photons from the innermost part of the disk body, while the latter is emitted via bremsstrahlung within the corona at relatively large radii. Furthermore, an inhomogeneous emissivity distribution over the disk produces humps in the microlens light curves because of enhanced microlens amplification of the bright areas. It is hoped that black-hole accretion theory coupled with future multi-wavelength microlens observations will be able to reveal such spatial and temporal behaviors of flows in the vicinity of black holes.

articleTitle: The Dense Plasma Torus around the Nucleus of an Active Galaxy NGC1052
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A subparsec-scale dense plasma torus around an active galactic nucleus is unveiled. We report on very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations at 2.3, 8.4, and 15.4 GHz towards the active galaxy NGC1052. The convex spectra of the double-sided jets and the nucleus imply that synchrotron emission is obscured through free–free absorption (FFA) by the foreground cold dense plasma. A trichromatic image was produced to illustrate the distribution of the FFA opacity. We found a central condensation of the plasma which covers about 0.1 pc and 0.7 pc of the approaching and receding jets, respectively. A simple explanation for the asymmetric distribution is the existence of a thick plasma torus perpendicular to the jets. We also found an ambient FFA absorber, whose density profile can be ascribed to a spherical distribution of the isothermal King model. The coexistence of torus-like and spherical distributions of the plasma suggests a transition from radial accretion to rotational accretion around the nucleus.

articleTitle: Subaru Deep Near-Infrared Imaging of the Field of a Possible Proto-Cluster Near the Radio Galaxy 53W002 at $z=2.4$
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of deep <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^\prime$</tex> - and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>-band imaging of the field of a proto-cluster region near the radio galaxy 53W002 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=2.390$</tex> with the Subaru Telescope. The data were analyzed together with deep optical and near-infrared (NIR) images taken with the Hubble Space Telescope to investigate the properties of ten optically compact emission-line galaxies and candidates. Excluding the three objects which may contain active galactic nuclei, many are faint or undetected at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$K^\prime$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lambda_{\rm rest} \approx 6000$</tex>Å), and are therefore revealed to be intrinsically small starbursting objects. On the other hand, we detect few objects with colors and magnitudes expected for quiescent massive galaxies at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z=2.4$</tex> in the field.

articleTitle: Multi-Phase Gas Dynamics in a Weak Barred Potential
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The structure of the interstellar medium in the central kpc region of a galaxy with a weak bar-like potential was investigated while taking into account realistic cooling and heating processes and the self-gravity of the gas. Using high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations, it has been revealed that the resonant structures (e.g. smooth spiral shocks and a nuclear ring) are very different from those seen in past numerical models where simple models of the ISM, i.e. non-self-gravitating, isothermal gas, were assumed. We find that the pc-scale filaments and clumps form large-scale spirals, which resemble those seen in real galaxies. The fine structures are different between the arms and in the nuclear region. The next-generation millimeter interferometer (ALMA) may reveal the fine structures of the cold gas in nearby galaxies. We also find a large-scale anisotropy in the gas temperature, which is caused by a non-circular velocity field of the gas. The damped-orbit model based on the epicyclic approximation explains the distribution of the hot (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gt 10^4 \, {\rm K}$</tex>) and cold (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\lt 100 \, {\rm K}$</tex>) gases appearing alternately around the galactic center. Because of the temperature anisotropy, cold gases observed by molecular lines do not necessarily represent the real gas distribution in galaxies. Position–Velocity diagrams strongly depend on the viewing angles. As a result, the rotational velocity inferred from the P–V maps could be two-times larger or smaller than the true circular velocity.

articleTitle: X-Ray Probing of the Central Regions of Clusters of Galaxies
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The results on ASCA X-ray study of the central regions of medium-richness clusters of galaxies are summarized, while emphasizing the differences between cD and non-cD clusters. The intra-cluster medium (ICM) is likely to consist of two (hot and cool) phases within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 100$</tex>kpc of a cD galaxy, where the ICM metallicity is also enhanced. In contrast, the ICM in non-cD clusters appears to be isothermal with a small metallicity gradient right of the center. The gravitational potential exhibits a hierarchical nesting around cD galaxies, while a total mass-density profile with a central cusp is indicated for a non-cD cluster, Abell 1060. The iron-mass-to-light ratio of the ICM decreases toward the center in both types of clusters, although it is radially constant in peripheral regions. The silicon-to-iron abundance ratio in the ICM increases with the cluster richness, but remains close to the solar ratio around cD galaxies. These overall results are interpreted without appealing to the popular cooling-flow hypothesis. Instead, an emphasis is put on the halo-in-halo structure formed around cD galaxies.

articleTitle: ASCA Deep Survey in the Lockman Hole Field
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of deep observations of the Lockman Hole field with the ASCA SIS, covering <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$926\,\rm{arcmin}^2$</tex> in the 1–7 keV energy range, with a sensitivity 3–5 times deeper than the previous ASCA larger area surveys. Utilizing the results of the ROSAT Ultra Deep survey, we have detected 32, 25, and 15 sources in the 1–7, 1–2, and 2–7 keV bands, and only 4, 4, and 1 sources remain unidentified, respectively. The average hardness of the sources detected in the 1–7 keV band with fluxes of between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{-14}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^{-13}\,\rm{erg}\,\rm{cm}^{-2}\,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> corresponds to a photon index of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.65\pm 0.10$</tex>. Type-2 AGNs show significantly harder spectra than type-1s, which can be explained by absorption column densities of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\rm{H}} \simeq 10^{22-23}\,\rm{cm}^{-2}$</tex> at the source redshifts. Fifteen sources are detected in the hard-band (2–7 keV), consisting of six type-1 AGNs, six type-2 AGNs, one star, one cluster of galaxies, and one unidentified source. Type-2 AGNs make up a major part of hard X-ray populations in the 2–7 keV band at a flux level of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3\times 10^{-14}\,\rm{erg}\,\rm{cm}^{-2}\,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> (2–7 keV). The redshift distributions of type-1 and type-2 AGNs suggest a lack of high luminosity (optically-defined) type-2 AGNs with intrinsic <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\rm H} \lt 10^{23}\,{\rm cm}^{-2}$</tex>, in the redshift range <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z\simeq 1$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2$</tex> and/or with intrinsic luminosities larger than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3\times 10^{44}\,\rm{erg}\,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> (2–10 keV at source frame).

articleTitle: Variable Line Profiles Due to Non-Axisymmetric Patterns in an Accretion Disc around a Rotating Black Hole
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have explored spectral line profiles due to spiral patterns in accretion discs around black holes. A parametrization was employed for the shape and emissivity of spiral waves, which can be produced by non-axisymmetric perturbations affecting the disc density and ionization structure. The effects of the light-travel time, energy shift, and gravitational focusing near to a rotating black hole were taken into account. A high-resolution ray-tracing code was used to follow the time variations of the synthetic line profile. A variety of expected spectral features were examined and the scheme applied to a broad iron line observed in MCG<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-$</tex>6–30–15.

articleTitle: Specifying the Environments around GRB, Explaining the Fe Line in the X-Ray Afterglow of GRB 000214
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a model for explaining the Fe K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> line and the continuum in the afterglow of GRB 000214. In this paper, we pose the importance to seek the physically natural environment around GRB 000214. For reproducing the observation, we need a ring-like remnant around the progenitor, like that of SN 1987A produced by the mass-loss of the progenitor and the fireball spread over all directions. The observation of GRB 000214, in which the continuum power-law spectrum decreased faster than the line, motivated us to consider two independent systems for the line emission and the continuum spectrum. At first, the continuum spectrum can be fitted by the afterglow emission of the fireball pointing toward the observer, which does not collide with the ring because the emission of GRB and the afterglow are highly collimated to the observer by the relativistic beaming effect. Secondly, the line can be fitted by the fluorescence of the Fe atoms in the ring illuminated by the X-ray afterglow. The significance of this study is that our model may strongly constrain the GRB model.

articleTitle: Revisiting the Faint Blue Galaxy Problem
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have investigated whether the pure luminosity evolution (PLE) model in a flat universe with cosmological constant <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Lambda$</tex> can explain the faint blue galaxy (FBG) problem in light of recent observations of a morphologically divided number count, redshift distribution, and color distribution. While the original FBG problem means an inconsistency between the total number count and redshift distribution at around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B > 22\, {\rm mag}$</tex>, we consider here the FBG problem in a broader context. In particular, we pay attention to an evolution model of irregular galaxies, of which predictions from the standard model disagree with recent observations. In addition to the standard 'S model' with slow star formation, we introduce a non-standard 'R model' with rapid star formation for irregular galaxies, and investigate the properties of the sum of these models (S+R model). The observed total number count and redshift distribution in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex>-band can be well reproduced by the PLE model in a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Lambda$</tex>-dominated universe. As for irregular galaxies, while the S model underproduces the observed count, the S+R model can account for the observation. Considering that the observed color distribution of faint irregular galaxies is very broad, we propose a possibility that irregular galaxies are composed of at least two populations.

articleTitle: HV Virginis and WZ Sge-Type Dwarf Novae
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A dwarf nova HV Vir was observed photometrically for eight nights during an outburst in 1992 April–May. The star showed two distinct types of periodic variation: (1) 82.20-min (0.05708d) double-humped variation with decaying amplitudes during the early stage of the outburst, and (2) 83.80-min (0.05820d) superhumps in later stages. We attributed the former to “early superhumps”, which are only seen in the earliest stage of WZ Sge-type outbursts. The superhump period and evolution of the superhumps, together with general characteristics of the light curve, make HV Vir a typical WZ Sge-type dwarf nova. HV Vir also showed a large increase of the superhump period during the superoutburst. Upon recognizing the WZ Sge-type nature of an object previously considered as a nova, we present a comprehensive list of candidates for WZ Sge-type dwarf novae and related systems.

articleTitle: Snapshot VLBI Observations of SiO v=1 and v=2 (J=1-0) Maser Sources
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have made snapshot VLBI observations of SiO masers of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J= 1$</tex>−0 transition at two vibrational levels <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v=1$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v=2$</tex> using the Kashima–Nobeyama Interferometer (KNIFE). Out of 37 sources observed, we detected both of the lines from 16 sources with a typical detection limit of 10 Jy. Most of the SiO masers were significantly spatially resolved with a KNIFE baseline (200 km), indicating extended/complicated structures of the SiO masers with a typical angular size of a few milliarcseconds. Similar fringe-phase profiles along a radial velocity spanning larger than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.0~\rm{km}~\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> between the two lines indicate a similar spatial structure along the velocity spacings. This tendency, shown from 13 SiO maser sources except Orion KL, supports spatial coincidence of the two lines found previously for M-type stars VY CMa and W Hya. The spatial coincidence should enable us to measure group-delays of the SiO masers for stellar astrometry.

articleTitle: ASCA Observations of the Temperature Structure and Metal Distribution in the Perseus Cluster of Galaxies
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Large-scale distributions of hot-gas temperature and Fe abundance in the Perseus cluster have been studied with multi-pointing observations by the GIS instrument onboard ASCA. Within a radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${20{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> from the cluster center, the energy spectra requires two temperature components, in which the cool component indicates <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT \sim 2\;\rm{keV}$</tex> and the hot-component temperature shows a significant decline from about 8 keV to 6 keV toward the center. In the outer region of the cluster, the temperature shows a fluctuation with an amplitude of about 2 keV, which suggest that a western region at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim {16{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> from the cluster center is relatively hotter. As for the Fe abundance, a significant decline with radius is detected from 0.44 solar at the center to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 0.1$</tex> solar at a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${50{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> offset region. If the observed Fe-K line intensity within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${4{}^{\rm {\prime }}}$</tex> from the center is suppressed by a factor of 2 due to the resonance scattering effect, the corrected Fe mass density follows the galaxy distribution. Finally, our results do not support the large-scale velocity gradients previously reported from the same GIS data.

articleTitle: Hubble Constant at Intermediate Redshift Using the CO-Line Tully-Fisher Relation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have determined distances and Hubble ratios for galaxies at intermediate redshifts, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$cz \sim 10000$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$35000 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, by applying the CO-line Tully–Fisher relation to our <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}CO (J=1 - 0)$</tex>-line observations using the Nobeyama 45-m telescope, and near-IR (NIR) photometry in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex> - and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H$</tex>-bands using the 1.88-m telescope at Okayama Astrophysical Observatory. By averaging the Hubble ratios from the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J$</tex>-band result, we obtained a Hubble constant of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$H_0 = 60 \pm 10 \rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1} \,\rm{Mpc}^{-1}$</tex>. We argue that the CO line–NIR Tully–Fisher relation can be a complimentary method to the other methods for measuring the distances of galaxies at intermediate and high redshifts.

articleTitle: The Gas-Drag Effect on the Orbital Instability of a Protoplanet System
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have investigated numerically the orbital instability of a protoplanet system while taking account of the gas-drag force due to the solar nebula. In the present work, we considered an equally spaced five-protoplanet (with the same mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1 \times 10^{-7} {{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>) system, in which their initial orbits are coplanar and circular, and assumed that the gas-drag force is proportional to the square of the relative velocity between the gas and a protoplanet. We first re-examined and confirmed that, under a gas-free condition, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\log_{10} T_{\rm{inst}}$</tex> can be approximately written as a linear function of the initial orbital separation distance, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta \tilde{a}_{0}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm{inst}}$</tex> is the time of the orbital instability (i.e., the time of the first orbital crossing between any two protoplanets). Next, we investigated the instability time under the gas-drag effect, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm{inst}}^{\rm{gas}}$</tex>, and found that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm{inst}}^{\rm{gas}}$</tex> suddenly becomes large compared with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm{inst}}$</tex>, when <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\Delta \tilde{a}}_{0}$</tex> is larger than a certain critical separation distance, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${({\Delta \tilde{a}}_{0})}_{\rm{crit}}$</tex>. Furthermore, we showed that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${({\Delta \tilde{a}}_{0})}_{\rm{crit}}$</tex> can be described semi-analytically as a function of the gaseous density. From a function extrapolated with a density in the minimum mass nebula model, we estimated <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${({\Delta \tilde{a}}_{0})}_{\rm{crit}}$</tex> in the nebula as being about 10 Hill radius at 1 AU.

articleTitle: A CO Outflow and a Molecular Cloud Core Associated with a Young Massive Star IRAS 22134$+$5834
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of the recent <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=1$</tex>-0), <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=1-0$</tex>), and C <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>O (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=1-0$</tex>) observations carried out toward a bright IRAS point source (22134<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5834) using the 45 m telescope at Nobeyama Radio Observatory (NRO) equipped with the 4 multi-beam receiver system. The IRAS source exhibits a cold color spectrum in the far infrared wavelengths and has a high luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 1700 \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex> at the adopted distance of 900 pc, indicating that the IRAS source is a good candidate for an embedded young massive star whose luminosity is equivalent to that of an early B-type star having <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 8 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. A bipolar outflow and a dense core associated with IRAS 22134<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$+$</tex>5834 were detected by the present observations. It is remarkable that the outflow has a very large total molecular mass of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$26 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, which makes this source one of the most massive outflows reported to date. We derived the dynamical time scale (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 7\times 10^4 \,\rm{yr}$</tex>), mechanical momentum (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 140 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}\,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>), and kinetic energy (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 400 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}} \,\rm{km}^2 \,\rm{s}^{-2}$</tex>) of the outflow. The dense core traced in C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>O is also massive (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$206 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>) extending over <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 1 \,\rm{pc}$</tex>. The core shows an elliptical shape with its major axis inclined by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-45 {{}^{\circ }}$</tex> to the north. A velocity gradient of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.9 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1} \,\rm{pc}^{-1}$</tex> along the core major axis was observed, indicating a rotation of the core. We also detected blue and red velocity-shifted components in C<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>O along the core minor axis separated by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\simeq 0.7 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex> from the systemic velocity at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-18.2 \,\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, which are most likely to trace the mixture of the dense gas being swept up by the powerful outflow and the matter in the core infalling toward the central star.

articleTitle: Sensitive CO Observations of the LMC Supergiant Shells with NANTEN: Their Effects on the Formation of Molecular Clouds and Stellar Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A statistical study of the effects of supergiant shells (SGSs) on the formation of stars and molecular clouds was made based on sensitive CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=1 \hbox{-} 0$</tex>) observations of the molecular clouds in the LMC with NANTEN. The sensitive observations have detected 168 CO clouds whose mass ranges from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 4 \times 10^4 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3 \times 10^6 \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. Out of the 168 clouds, 63 are associated with the SGSs, accounting for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gtrsim 35\%$</tex>. The surface number and mass densities of the CO clouds are higher by a factor of 1.5–2 at the edge of the SGSs than elsewhere. This suggests the formation of CO clouds under the dynamical effects of the SGSs, such as the accumulation of interstellar medium. Young stellar clusters are more actively formed on the side of the CO clouds facing to the center of the SGSs, particularly where the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${\rm H} \alpha$</tex> filaments are adjacent to the CO clouds. The number of clusters is increased by a factor of 2 on the side facing to the center of the SGSs with respect to the CO peaks compared with on the side far from the center. These results strongly suggest that cluster formation is triggered by dynamical effects of the SGSs. We find that <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 60\%$</tex> of the young clusters are located within the boundary of the SGSs, and propose that a few 10% of the young clusters of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\tau \lt 10 \, {\rm Myr}$</tex> have likely been formed due to dynamical effects of the SGSs.

articleTitle: Dynamic Current Injection into Magnetic Loops in Active Regions II. A 3D Magnetodynamic Model for Loop Flares
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have studied propagation along magnetic flux tubes in the active-region corona of large-amplitude torsional Alfvén wave packets (TAWP’s) coming up from a subphotospheric convection zone. TAWP’s can serve to transfer magnetic energy from the high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta (\beta = P_{\rm{g}}/P_{\rm{m}})$</tex> subphotospheric region to the low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> coronal region. They dump part (or all) of their energy in the low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> coronal region, which may result in very high temperature-plasma observed in X-rays (and in high energy particles). The supply of TAWPs from the photosphere, considered to be inefficient because the Alfvén velocity in the photosphere is small, turns out to be sufficiently effective for large-amplitude TAWP’s. This is due to the magnetic buoyancy acting on the magnetic twist packet and to the non-linear effect of squeezing out the gas from the twisted part of loops when it comes up near the photosphere. Both of these effects enhance the speed of emergence of the twist. We propose that loop flares may be due to the transport of energy and mass by torsional Alfvén waves. They may be the result of energy conversion of the magnetic twists and the kinetic energy of the accelerated hypersonic flows into thermal energy when two such TAWP’s collide high in a coronal loop. In order for such a collision of TAWP’s to occur, a TAWP is injected from one footpoint of a loop whilst another TAWP, from the other footpoint, is still propagating along the loop. The collision of these two TAWP’s at a high part of the loop explains the creation of a hyperhot region. The acceleration of high-energy particles is also explained as being due to the Fermi-I process between the approaching two hypersonic magnetic shocks.

articleTitle: 2 Millimeter Dust around NGC 7538 — IRS 1, 2, and 3: I. Unfilled Structure of Dust Cloud
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A 2-mm continuum mapping observation around NGC 7538 — IRS 1, 2, and 3 was made by the Nobeyama Bolometer Array (NOBA) with a spatial resolution of 12<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime\prime}$</tex>. An extended source of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim {32{}^{\rm {\prime \prime }}} \times {44{}^{\rm {\prime \prime }}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\Delta\alpha \times \Delta\delta$</tex>), having a hardly resolved central core structure, was observed. The core gives a flux density of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.1 \,\rm{Jy} \pm 1 \,\rm{Jy}$</tex>, and is clearly identified with the free-free emission from the compact H II regions. A smooth and extended source gives an integrated flux density of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$5 \,\rm{Jy} \pm 1.5 \,\rm{Jy}$</tex>, and an intensity spectrum of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\nu^{3}$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\nu^{3.5}$</tex> in the millimeter wave region. The fitting of a gray body function to the observational data shows that an absorption index, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex>, of 1.8–2.0, a dust filling factor, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\eta$</tex>, of 0.3–0.5, and a dust temperature, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm d}$</tex>, of 34 K–45 K are reasonable parameters for this 2-mm extended dust. Astronomical silicate grains were examined for a dust model. The total dust mass and luminosity were obtained as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm d} \simeq 0.85 \times 10^{2} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm d} \simeq 2.2 \times 10^{5} \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, respectively. The extent of 2-mm dust emission partly coincides with those of the 100-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/mu$</tex> m map, of the 57-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$/mu$</tex> m map, and of the total intensity of the wing parts of the CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1-0$</tex>) line emission of the region. The absorbing silicate dust layer must be distinct from the extended 2-mm dust, and must arise on smaller scales than the extended 2-mm dust.

articleTitle: A CO Survey of the LMC with NANTEN: III. Formation of Stellar Clusters and Evolution of Molecular Clouds
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to elucidate star formation in the LMC, we made a complete study of CO clouds with NANTEN. In the present paper, we compare 55 giant molecular clouds (GMCs), whose physical quantities were well determined, with young objects, such as young stellar clusters and H ii regions. We find that the GMCs are actively forming stars and clusters; 23 and 40 are found to be associated with the clusters and the H ii regions, respectively. The clusters associated with the GMCs are significantly young; <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 85\%$</tex> of them are younger than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10 \,\rm{Myr}$</tex>. In addition, compact groups of the young clusters are often found at the peak position of the GMCs, e.g., N 159 and N 44, while much looser groups are away from the GMCs. This suggests that the clusters are formed in groups and disperse as they become old. The distributions of the CO, [C ii], and UV indicate that the GMCs are likely to be rapidly dissipated within several Myr due to UV photons from the clusters. We also estimate the evolutionary time scale of the GMCs; they form stars in a few Myr after their birth, and form clusters during the next few Myr, and are dissipated in the subsequent few Myr.

articleTitle: Solar Models with Helioseismic Constraints and the Solar Neutrino Problem
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Imposing a constraint of the sound-speed profile determined from helioseismology and updating the microphysics, we have revised our seismic solar model, constructed with the assumption of a homogeneous metal abundance distribution, and have shown that the theoretically expected neutrino fluxes are still significantly more than the observations. With the same sound-speed profile constraint, we also constructed solar models with low metal abundance in the core, and evaluated the neutrino fluxes of these models to see if nonstandard solar models with a low metal core can solve the solar neutrino problem. Some of these models are in agreement with the Homestake data, the Super-Kamiokande data, and the sound-speed profile simultaneously, but none of these satisfy both the neutrino flux data, including GALLEX and SAGE, and the helioseismically determined density profile.

articleTitle: Subaru Deep Survey I. Near-Infrared Observations
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Deep near-infrared images of a blank 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\prime}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \times$</tex> 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ ^{\prime}$</tex> section of sky near the galactic north pole taken by Subaru Telescope are presented. The total integration times of the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K^{\prime}$</tex> bands were 12.1 hr and 9.7 hr, resulting in 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ \sigma$</tex> limiting magnitudes of 25.1 and 23.5 mag, respectively. The numbers of sources within these limiting magnitudes found with an automated detection procedure are 385 in the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex> band and 350 in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K^{\prime}$</tex>. Based on photometric measurements of these sources, we present number count vs. magnitude relations, color vs. magnitude diagrams, size vs. color relationships, etc. The slope of the galaxy number count plotted against the AB magnitude scale is about 0.23 in the 22 to 26 AB magnitude range of both bands. The spatial number density of galaxies as well as the slopes in the faint-end region given by the Subaru Deep Field (SDF) survey are consistent with those given by HST-NICMOS surveys, as expressed on the AB magnitude diagram. Several sources having very large <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J - K^{\prime}$</tex> color have been found, including a few <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ K^{\prime}$</tex> objects without detection at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ J$</tex>. In addition, a number of faint galactic stars were also detected, most of which are assigned to M-subdwarfs, together with a few brown dwarf candidates.

articleTitle: Interpolation of One - and Two-Dimensional Images with Pixelwise Photon Number Conservation
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The interpolation of one - and two-dimensional images is considered. The usual linear or cubic spline interpolations try to connect given data points. On the other hand, image data give area integrals of the radiation intensity (i.e., photon counts) over pixels. Based on variational principles, we have developed schemes of quadratic and fourth-order polynomial interpolation which reproduce the given pixelwise photon counts exactly. These methods were tested on some simple examples and showed satisfactory results.

articleTitle: Detection of Eight Molecular Supershells in the Southern Milky Way with NANTEN
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
