abstract: We carried out a new CO survey for molecular supershells in the southern Milky Way with NANTEN. We covered an area of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$300^{\circ} \lt l \lt 350^{\circ}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-9^{\circ} \lt b \lt 9^{\circ}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4^{\prime}$</tex> or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$8^{\prime}$</tex> grid spacings with a 2.<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex>6 beamsize. In addition to the disk component at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\vert b\vert \lt 2^{\circ}$</tex>, we found numerous filamentary or arc-like CO distributions by inspecting the velocity channel maps. As a result, we identified 8 supershell candidates, 3 of which are associated with CO holes in the galactic disk. Six of the supershells had not been identified by the previous studies, while 2 of them were known from H i and low-resolution CO surveys. The size of the supershells ranges from 100 pc to 450 pc and the average is 230 pc; their age ranges from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.2 \times 10^6 \;\rm{yr}$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.1 \times 10^7 \,\rm{yr}$</tex>. We note that two of the supershells are also associated with observable indications of supershells at other wavelengths, including H i, far-infrared, soft X-ray, and SNRs. The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of the impact of supershells on star formation in the Galaxy.

articleTitle: The Most Massive C18O Molecular Complex in Centaurus and Star Formation Therein
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: New observations of the <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sup>CO, <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">13</sup>CO, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J = 1 \hbox{-} 0$</tex>) emission lines have been extensively made toward the Centaurus tangential region <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$({308\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}5} \le l \le {310\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}5}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$- {1\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}0} \le b \le {1\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}0})$</tex> using the “NANTEN”telescope. These observations have revealed a massive molecular complex in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 1.8 \times 10^{5}\,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>, the most massive one observed in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{C}{{18\atop} \rm{O}}$</tex> to date in the Galaxy. This complex is highly elongated with a size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 80 \,\rm{pc} \times \sim 25 \,\rm{pc}$</tex> at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$309^{\circ} \le l \le {309\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}5}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$- {0\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}9} \le b \le {0\rlap {.}{}^{\rm {\circ }}4}$</tex>, including 35 dense molecular clumps whose mass ranges from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4.7 \times 10^{2} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.4 \times 10^{4} \,{{{M}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. Twenty-seven of the 35 clumps are associated with IRAS point sources whose luminosity ranges from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$7.2 \times 10^{2} \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex> to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$3.6 \times 10^{5} \,{{{L}_{\odot}}}$</tex>. We find that the luminosity of the candidate protostellar IRAS sources is well correlated with the molecular line width, as fitted by a power law, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\log (L_{\rm IRAS}) = 1.1 + (9.2 \pm 0.6) \log (\Delta V)$</tex>. This suggests that the mass of the formed stars is determined by the internal velocity dispersion of the dense cores. A comparison with an H I distribution shows that the molecular gas forms a ring-like structure inside an H I hole of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 55 \hbox{-} 70 \;\rm{pc}$</tex> radius. Since the H I gas surrounding the hole shows a signature of expansion at several <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rm{km} \,\rm{s}^{-1}$</tex>, we suggest that the H I hole exhibits a shell created by some explosive events, like supernovae, during the last <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim (6 \hbox{-} 8) \times 10^{6} \,\rm{yr}$</tex>. The ring-like structure of the CO distribution may be found due to the interaction between the expanding shell and the interstellar medium, leading to a trigger of massive star formation.

articleTitle: Slim Disk: Viscosity Prescriptions and Observational Implications
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We examine how different viscosity prescriptions and magnitudes affect the structure of the slim disk. Unlike the case with a standard disk, radiation from the slim disk is influenced by the viscosity parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, in such a way that the estimated maximum effective temperature of the disk slightly increases as <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> increases. This is because the larger is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>, the larger does the accretion velocity become and, hence, the more enhanced does the advective energy transport become, which means less efficient radiative cooling and thus higher temperatures. Furthermore, we checked different viscosity prescriptions with the form of the viscous stress tensor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_{r \varphi} =-\alpha \beta^{\mu}p_{\rm total}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\beta$</tex> is the ratio of the gas pressure to the total pressure, and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex> is a parameter (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0 \le \mu \le 1$</tex>). In contrast with the case with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu=0$</tex>, which shows significant decrease in the inner-edge radius and the flattering of the effective temperature profile at high luminosities, for large <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>, say <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu \sim 0.5$</tex>, neither of the inner-edge of the disk nor temperature profiles does not appreciably change even at the Eddington luminosity. We can rule out a case with large <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu~(\sim 0.5)$</tex>, since it would not be able to produce a drop in the inner-edge radius of an increase in the luminosity, as was observed in an ultraluminous X-ray source, IC 342, source 1
